To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

picomole amounts (1-100 pmol) of protein, separated by one- and two-dimentional gel electrophoreses, can be sequenced after electroblotting onto nitrocelluose, in situ proteolytic digestion of the electroblotted protein, and separation of the resulting peptides by reverse-phase HPL C.

picomole quantities (0.5-1.5 pmol) of protein can be sequenced after separation by one- and two-dimentional polyacrylamid gel electrophoreses, in situ protease digestions on nitrocelluose and reverse phase HPLC separations of the resulting peptide mixtures.

picomole quantities (1-10 micrograms) of proteins separated by polyacrylamid gel electrophoreses can be subjected to internal amino acid sequence analysis after electroblotting onto nitrocelluose and in situ digestion with trypsin or V-8 proteases, followed by HPLC purification of the resulting peptide fragments and gas-phase sequence analysis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new techniques to facilitate protein structure analysis.
developing methods for the separation and analysis of complex protein mixtures, with the aim of providing tools for the analysis of gene expression.
the development of methods for the analysis of proteins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the method is a powerful tool for obtaining sequence data from proteins separated by gel-electrophoretic techniques.
the method is simple to perform and has proven to be a valuable tool for the analysis of proteins separated on polyacrylamides gels.

the method is applicable to any protein that has been successfully separated by one- and two-dimen- sional gel electrophoreses, and the method has been successfully utilized for the sequence determination of more than 100 different proteins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the method has worked for every protein that we have tried to sequence.
we can now routinely obtain internal sequence information from 10-50 pmol of any protein of interest.
we can now obtain amino acid sequence data for any protein of interest from any source, including tissues, cell cultures, or purified preparations, and from as little as 10(4)-10(5) molecules.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can now sequence a protein from a gel.
the combination of in situ protease digestions and HPLC separations can be used to obtain amino acid sequence information from a wide range of picomole quantities (0.2-10 pmol) of proteins.
it is possible to obtain internal amino acid sequence from a picomole of protein separated by one- and two-dimension polyacrylamid gel electrophoreses.
